title: Let’s meet up
blurb: Inviting, arranging, and a model email

Warm-up: The invitation that never became a date is universal. Four answers, then move on.
Vocabulary: Make it, book a table, call back, miss a call are learned whole.
Free = not busy, and free = costing nothing. Both are true; only the first matters today.
Grammar: This is a phrase bank with a shape, not a paradigm. Do not turn it into one.
The refusal is the hard part
Students can invite. They cannot refuse politely. Spend the time on I’m afraid I can’t… plus a reason plus an alternative.
Only two uses at this level: offers and suggestions with I or we. Say it once.
Practice: Exercise 3 is about tone, not grammar. The direct versions are not wrong in form.
Exercise 6 brings back going to and the Present Continuous from Lesson 11. Name it as recycling.
Listening: 4.11 is two messages nobody answers. Ask what each caller wants before playing 4.12.
4.12 is the same two situations resolved. The pairing is the point.
Nine phrases in the speakers’ own voices. Play them again before the role play.
The model: They are looking for the parts they will reuse, not answering comprehension questions.
Accepting is easy. The model shows how to refuse and offer an alternative in two lines.
Now you: Each student sees only their own card. Do not let them read each other’s.
The second run is where the language is learned. Do not cut it for time.
One phrase used well, one to try next time.
Wrap: Both future forms came back today, in Practice 6 and throughout the role play.
Next is the Unit 4 Test. Tell them they can take it as many times as they like.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Inviting, refusing, fixing

Three jobs, and a phrase for each. The middle one is the difficult one.

Read these four lines from the recordings.
  • Would you like to meet for lunch?
  • Do you fancy doing something this weekend?
  • I’m afraid I can’t make the 28th.
  • How about the 29th instead?
Look at the first two. What comes after each one?
What do you want to do?
The jobThe phraseWhat follows it
Check somebody is freeAre you free…? · Are you doing anything…?on Friday · that week · tomorrow evening
Invite — more formalWould you like to…?to + verb: Would you like to meet for lunch?
Invite — more casualDo you fancy…?-ing: Do you fancy doing something?
Suggest a time or a planHow about…? · Shall we…? · Could we…?How about + noun or -ing · Shall we / Could we + plain verb
AcceptThat’d be lovely. · Sounds great! · Yes, I’d like to very much. · That works for me.
Refuse politelyI’m afraid I can’t make Thursday — then a reason — then an alternative: I’m working. Is Sunday any good for you?
Fix itShall we say eight? · Shall we meet outside the restaurant? · I’ll confirm nearer the time.
Future forms recycledan arrangement uses the Present Continuous: I’m working tomorrow; an intention uses going to: I’m going to book a table

TWO PATTERNS TO KEEP APART. Would you like to meet? but Do you fancy meeting? Same job, different shape.

REFUSING HAS THREE PARTS. The apology, the reason, the alternative. Leave any one of them out and it sounds cold.

The mistake to watch: I can’t come on its own. Add the reason and an alternative day, or the invitation dies there.

TWO WAYS TO INVITE. Would you like to…? is neutral and works with anybody, including people you do not know well. Do you fancy…? is casual and for friends. The shapes are different: would like takes to + verb, fancy takes the -ing form.

SUGGESTING. How about takes a noun or an -ing form: How about Friday? / How about meeting at eight? Shall we and Could we take the plain verb: Shall we say eight?

REFUSING POLITELY HAS THREE PARTS. 1) the apology — I’m afraid I can’t make Thursday; 2) the reason — I’m working; 3) the alternative — Is Sunday any good for you? A refusal with only part 1 sounds like you do not want to come.

CONFIRMING. Repeat the arrangement back so both of you have the same information: So we’re meeting outside the restaurant at eight on Sunday.

Two mistakes to watch: Do you fancy to go? (fancy takes -ing) and a bare No, I can’t, which ends the conversation.

This is the same politeness pattern you will meet again in Lesson 15, where you complain and ask for a refund.

Listen and read. Five phrases from the recordings, one at a time.

Navigate B1 · Audio 4.13 — the phrases in the speakers’ own voices.

Full grammar reference — Inviting, refusing and arranging

Form

InvitingDo you fancy + -ing? · How about + -ing? · Would you like to + verb? · Shall we + verb?
Asking about the diaryAre you free on Friday? · Are you doing anything on Saturday?
AcceptingThat sounds great. · That works for me. · I’d love to.
Refusing politelyI’m afraid I can’t make it — I’m working. How about Sunday?
ConfirmingSo, Friday at eight? · See you then.

When and why we use it

  • A polite refusal has three parts: sorry → reason → new suggestion. Leaving out the third part sounds cold.
  • Do you fancy…? and How about…? are followed by -ing; Would you like…? and Shall we…? are followed by the plain verb.
  • Arrangements are talked about in the Present Continuous: I’m meeting my sister then.
  • Always confirm the final time in one short sentence.

Signal words

on Friday · at eight · instead · nearer the time

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Do you fancy to go? → Do you fancy going?Fancy + -ing.
  • How about to meet? → How about meeting?How about + -ing.
  • I can’t make. → I can’t make it.The phrase needs it.
  • Shall we to go? → Shall we go?No to after shall.

Don’t confuse it with

Would you like to…? is the more formal invitation; Do you fancy…? is for friends.

Stage 6 · The model

The invitation, and the reply

Two short emails. The second one is the one worth copying.

Read both emails. You are reading them as a writer — look for the parts you can reuse.

The invitation

Subject: Saturday the 12th?

Hi Aigerim,

It’s been ages! I’m organising a small dinner for Marat’s birthday on Saturday the 12th, at that Georgian place on the seafront. We’re meeting at seven thirty.

Do you fancy coming? Let me know by Wednesday so I can book a table.

See you soon,
Dana

Note. Written for this course as a pair of writing models. The two emails and the people in them are invented.

Two short messages to a friend

The reply

Subject: Re: Saturday the 12th?

Hi Dana,

Thanks for the invitation — that sounds lovely.

I’m afraid I can’t make seven thirty: I’m working until eight. Could we say eight thirty instead? If that doesn’t fit in, I’ll come another time and bring his present round separately.

Let me know and I’ll confirm with Marat.

Anyway, speak soon,
Aigerim

Stage 7 · Now you

Now you

Invite somebody, get refused, and fix it anyway.One of you invites. Then you swap.One of you invites. Then you swap.

Useful language
  • Inviting: Are you free on…? · Are you doing anything on…? · Would you like to…? · Do you fancy…-ing?
  • Accepting: That’d be lovely. · Sounds great! · That works for me. · Yes, I’d like to very much.
  • Refusing: I’m afraid I can’t make… · I’m really sorry, but… · (then a reason, then an alternative)
  • Suggesting: How about…? · Is… any good for you? · Could we… instead? · Shall we say…?
  • Fixing it: Shall we meet outside…? · I’ll book a table. · I’ll email you to confirm.
1 · Work in pairs. Read your card only. Do not show it to your partner.
Card A · you invite

It is your sister’s birthday on Friday the 20th. You are organising dinner at a restaurant near the seafront at eight. Your goal: get your partner to come, and agree who books the table. You cannot change the day.

Card B · you are invited

You want to go, but you are working until nine on Friday the 20th, and you are away the whole weekend after it. Your goal: find a way to see them without saying a flat no.

2 · Work in pairs. Have the conversation. Use the Useful language box.

Do not write a script. Start with Are you doing anything on Friday the 20th? and see where it goes.

3 · Swap cards and do it again with the second situation.
Card C · you invite

You are new in the company and want to take a colleague to lunch. You are only in the city the week of the 27th. Your goal: fix a day and a place, and be polite — you do not know this person well.

Card D · you are invited

You are pleased to be asked, but you have meetings on the 27th and the 28th. Your goal: accept warmly, refuse those two days politely, and end the call with a date in the diary.
